analysis.one_liner: Would have forced cable companies to open their broadband lines to any Internet provider customers choose.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Commerce Committee and its telecom subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: In the late 1990s, cable companies were building the fastest way onto the Internet — but many required customers to use the cable company's own Internet service. This bill would have let the Federal Communications Commission require cable operators to carry any Internet provider on fair, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory terms, and to treat cable-provided telecom service as a common carrier service subject to regulation. It would also have preserved cities' power to require open access when granting cable franchises.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who wanted high-speed Internet through their chosen provider instead of paying the cable company's affiliated provider — the bill's own findings note that customers wanting their own ISP on a cable line had to 'pay twice'. Independent Internet service providers (ISPs) would also gain direct access to cable customers, and cities acting as local cable franchising authorities would keep their ability to require open access.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes the FCC to require cable operators to offer Internet interconnection on terms that are 'fair, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory', including direct interconnection with the facilities of any ISP whether or not affiliated with the cable operator [S2][S3].

The bill's findings state that some cable operators required customers to take broadband only through the cable operator's affiliated ISP, and that customers who wanted their own ISP had to pay twice — once to the cable operator's ISP and once to their own [S3].

Declares that a telecommunications service provided by a cable system is subject to regulation as a common carrier service, extending non-discrimination rules to cable-provided telecom services [S2][S3].

Expands leased-access channel rules to cover non-video services, letting high-speed data providers obtain cable channel capacity under the same rules as commercial users until the FCC sets open-access standards [S2][S3].

Expressly preserves the authority of states and local franchising authorities, citing Portland, Oregon's open-access requirement upheld by a federal court, so cities could keep serving as 'laboratories' for competition [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators — companies like the ones building cable broadband networks in 1999 — would lose the ability to steer every high-speed customer to their own affiliated Internet service, and would have to share their network with rival ISPs at regulator-set terms. Customers of cable broadband could face somewhat higher access fees if cable companies passed on the cost of carrying competing ISPs, though competition among ISPs would push in the other direction.

drawbacks.text: Cable operators and economists argued at the time that forcing cable networks to open to rivals would reduce the incentive to build out broadband infrastructure and slow deployment of high-speed service — a concern the bill itself acknowledges in its findings [S3].

The bill hands significant discretion to the FCC to set interconnection terms after notice and comment, which could have produced lengthy regulatory proceedings and litigation over what counts as 'fair, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory' terms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is the classic one in network regulation: forcing the company that built the wire to share it lowers prices and preserves consumer choice, but may somewhat weaken the incentive to build. In 1999, cable broadband was essentially the only high-speed consumer option in most areas, and the bill addressed a real problem its own text documents — customers forced to 'pay twice' to reach the ISP of their choice. The design leans on FCC rulemaking rather than immediate mandates, and preserves local authority rather than overriding it, which moderates the risks.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 1999, sent to the House Commerce Committee, referred to its telecommunications subcommittee a month later, and then sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Representative Earl Blumenauer introduced the Consumer and Community Choice in Access Act of 1999 on July 29, 1999, joined by Representative Peter DeFazio [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce [S5].
On August 27, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection — the last action recorded [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable broadband operators came out ahead: by keeping the bill in committee, they avoided a requirement to share their networks with independent ISPs and preserved their affiliated-ISP business model for the remaining life of the 106th Congress. Consumers who wanted a choice of Internet provider on cable lines gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require cable operators to open broadband lines to unaffiliated ISPs.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce (106th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 29, 1999 and referred it to its telecommunications subcommittee; took no further action, never scheduling a hearing or vote.

against.name: Cable broadband industry
against.role: Cable operators and their affiliated ISPs (e.g., AT&T, Comcast, Time Warner)
against.what_they_did: Opposed government-mandated 'open access'/'forced access' rules for cable broadband and argued such rules would slow network buildout, during the same period the bill was pending.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Oregon Democrats, but the bill attracted only one cosponsor and never reached a vote, so the record shows no partisan split on support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped cable operators of exclusive control over which ISP reaches their subscribers, ending the affiliated-ISP model the bill's findings describe. Their gain from the bill's failure was keeping the cable line as a closed gateway to high-speed Internet.

ISPs like the ones locked out of cable networks would have gained direct, nondiscriminatory access to cable broadband customers, and customers would no longer pay twice to reach them. The bill's failure left these providers confined to slower phone-line technologies.
Cable companies' own Internet services (the model the bill targeted) would have lost their guaranteed captive subscriber base on the fastest consumer Internet platform of the era.
